Social Preview Checker

Fetches a page's Open Graph and Twitter Card meta tags plus the real pixel dimensions of its preview image, and classifies the result into the problems that actually break a shared link: missing og:title/og:description/image, a relative og:image URL (Open Graph requires it be absolute), an image below the platform's size minimum, a missing twitter:card, a duplicated tag, and an og:url that doesn't match the page you checked. Applies the twitter:image → og:image fallback chain correctly instead of flagging a missing twitter:image as a problem on its own.

1. Run the CLI against your page

Node.js, no dependencies to install:

node cli/check.mjs https://example.com/your-page --json

Get check.mjs, probe.mjs, analyze.mjs, metatags.mjs and imagesize.mjs from the repo — plain Node, nothing to install. It only ever talks to the URL you pass and whatever it points its preview image at; nothing goes through this site.

2. Paste the JSON output here

Paste the JSON from step 1 and click Check.

Report

Tags this tool read

Bonus: check any image URL's real dimensions, no CLI needed

Loading an <img> element (unlike fetching its bytes) is not subject to CORS, so this works for a third-party image URL directly in this page -- nothing is uploaded, the image loads straight from its own host to your browser.

Common questions

Why does my og:image not show up on LinkedIn or Slack even though it works on Facebook?

The most common cause this tool catches is a relative og:image URL (like /images/preview.png instead of https://example.com/images/preview.png). The Open Graph protocol requires og:image to be an absolute URL, and crawlers differ in how forgivingly they handle a relative one -- some resolve it against the page URL, others simply fail to load an image at all. The second most common cause is the image being below the platform's minimum size, which some crawlers reject outright rather than upscale. More detail: the fallback chain and size-rule reference.

Do I need a separate twitter:image tag, or does og:image work on X/Twitter too?

You don't strictly need one. Twitter/X's card renderer falls back to og:image when twitter:image is absent (and to og:title/og:description for those tags too), so a page with only Open Graph tags set can still render correctly there. This tool follows that fallback chain rather than reporting a missing twitter:image as a problem on its own -- it only becomes one if the og:image it falls back to has its own issue (too small, unreachable, relative).

What image size does Facebook actually require?

Facebook's own sharing documentation states a minimum of 200x200 pixels, below which the image is commonly not rendered at all, and a recommended size of 1200x630 pixels (a 1.91:1 ratio) for a full-size preview. Platform rendering behaviour is not contractually guaranteed and can change without notice -- treat these as strong, documented defaults rather than an absolute promise.

What image size does Twitter/X's summary_large_image card require?

Twitter's card documentation states a minimum of 300x157 pixels for the large-image card, below which it commonly falls back to a smaller layout or shows nothing, and a recommended size of 1200x628 pixels (roughly a 2:1 ratio).

Why does this need a CLI instead of just checking a URL I type into the page?

Fetching an arbitrary third-party page's HTML from inside a browser tab is blocked by CORS unless that site opts in with an Access-Control-Allow-Origin header, which almost none do -- the same restriction every other response-probing tool in this portfolio runs into. A small local CLI with no such restriction, run from your own machine, does the actual fetching. The one thing the browser CAN do on its own is check an image's real pixel dimensions, since loading an <img> element (unlike a fetch() of its bytes) is not subject to CORS -- this page's third tool does exactly that.

Does a clean report mean my link preview will definitely render correctly everywhere?

No. This checks a specific, documented set of Open Graph and Twitter Card patterns from one page fetch -- it is not a guarantee of how any individual platform's crawler will render the result today, since platforms cache aggressively, sometimes require a manual cache-refresh (LinkedIn's Post Inspector, for instance), and can change their rendering rules without notice. Treat a clean report as evidence these specific, well-documented patterns are correct, not a determination that every platform's preview will look a particular way.

Evidence, not a determination. This checks a specific, documented set of Open Graph and Twitter Card patterns from one page fetch. It is not a guarantee of how any individual platform will render the result today -- platforms cache aggressively and can change rendering rules without notice. A clean report describes what this one fetch found, not a promise about every platform's preview.

The page you're reading now only parses JSON you paste into it, and loads an image URL you paste into it, locally; nothing is uploaded anywhere this tool controls. Podcast Feed Validator checks your show's RSS feed against Apple Podcasts' documented requirements, the same "check what you're about to publish" idea applied to a feed instead of a page. social-preview-fallback-rules.html.text:
Fix a broken social link preview

← Back to Social Preview Checker

A shared link with no image, the wrong image, or no title almost always comes down to one of five things. Check them in this order -- each one can hide the next.

1. Make og:image an absolute URL

The Open Graph protocol (ogp.me) requires og:image to be an absolute URL, not a path relative to the page. A tag like <meta property="og:image" content="/images/preview.png"> is invalid per spec — some crawlers resolve it against the page URL anyway, others do not, so a relative URL is the single most common cause of an image silently failing to appear.

2. The fallback chain: twitter:* falls back to og:*

You don't need separate twitter:image, twitter:title, and twitter:description tags. X/Twitter's card renderer falls back to the matching og:* tag when its own is absent. What you do need is an explicit twitter:card value (summary or summary_large_image) — whether X falls back to plain Open Graph tags with no twitter:card at all is undocumented and has changed before, so set it explicitly rather than relying on that.

3. Meet the platform's documented minimum image size

Platform / card typeDocumented minimumRecommended
Facebook / LinkedIn (og:image)200 x 200 px1200 x 630 px (1.91:1)
Twitter/X summary_large_image300 x 157 px1200 x 628 px (~2:1)

Below the hard minimum, an image is commonly not rendered at all rather than shown smaller. Check your actual served file's pixel dimensions, not the source image you started from — a build step or CDN resize can quietly shrink it below the line. This checker fetches the real bytes and reads the dimensions out of the file header rather than trusting an og:image:width tag, which can go stale independently of the file it describes.

4. Check for a duplicated tag from a CMS or SEO plugin

Many platforms (WordPress SEO plugins especially) inject their own og:title/og:image tags, which can collide with a hand-written tag already in the template. Most crawlers use the first matching tag in document order, but which one that is depends on which system rendered its tag first in the final HTML — view the page's actual source (not the CMS editor) to see which value wins.

5. Force a re-fetch on the platform you're testing

Every major platform caches a link's preview aggressively and will keep showing a stale (or blank) result after you fix the tags until it re-crawls the URL. Use that platform's own preview-refresh tool where one exists before concluding your fix did not work — this checker reads the tags and image as they are right now, not what a platform's cache currently shows a visitor.

Evidence, not a determination. The size and fallback rules above reflect each platform's own published documentation at the time this was written. Platforms change rendering behaviour without notice, and this page is not a guarantee that a given fix will render correctly on any specific platform today.

No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is not marketing, SEO, or legal advice. vs-checking-tags-by-eye.html.text:
← Social Preview Checker

Social Preview Checker vs. checking your tags by eye

Opening view-source or DevTools' Elements panel and reading the og: and twitter: meta tags is the method most developers reach for first, and it is a real, free way to catch the most obvious failure: a tag that is missing outright. This page names no company or product -- reading a page's own markup is a generic habit every web developer already has, not a tool being compared against.

Check your page's tags →

That habit works well for exactly the case it is suited to: is the tag there at all. It runs into trouble the moment the question becomes anything more specific than presence -- is the image actually big enough, is the URL actually absolute, and is there exactly one of each tag rather than two fighting for the same platform's attention? None of those three are visible from reading the tag's text.

What each method actually tells you.
QuestionReading the tags by eyeThis checker
Is an og:image (or twitter:image) tag present at all? Catches it -- a missing tag is visible in the markup. Catches it too.
Is the image behind that tag actually large enough for Facebook's or Twitter's documented minimum? Not visible from the tag's text -- the URL string says nothing about the file's real pixel dimensions. Fetches the image and reads its real width/height from the file's own header.
Is the og:image URL absolute, as the Open Graph protocol requires, rather than relative? Easy to miss -- a relative URL opens fine in your own browser tab, because your browser resolves it against the page you're on. Flags a relative URL explicitly, before any platform's crawler has a chance to fail resolving it with no page context.
Did a CMS plugin write a second og:title (or similar) alongside your theme's own tag? Both tags look equally valid sitting in the markup; which one a parser keeps isn't visible from reading either one. Reports duplicated tags for the same property as a distinct finding.
Is a missing twitter:image actually a problem, given the documented og:* fallback chain? Reads as broken at a glance, which invites "fixing" it with a second image tag to keep in sync by hand. Applies the fallback chain first, and only flags the case where the fallback itself has nothing to fall back to.
Run the same check the same way every time, right before a page ships? Manual, and only as thorough as whoever is looking that day. A CLI with a real exit code, or the browser report viewer on this page.

A quick look at the markup is still worth doing -- it is free, it needs no tool, and it genuinely catches the tag-is-missing case in seconds. What it cannot do is answer the three questions above that decide whether a preview actually renders, which is the gap this checker exists to close.

Common questions

What does reading the tags by eye actually catch?

Opening a page's view-source or DevTools' Elements panel and scanning for og:title, og:description, og:image, and the twitter: equivalents is a real, fast way to catch the most obvious failure: a tag that is simply missing. If og:image isn't in the markup at all, you'll see that in seconds with no tool.

Where does eyeballing the tags fall short?

Three ways this checker catches and a by-eye read of the markup cannot, even by a careful reader: (1) the og:image tag can be present and point at a real image that is simply too small -- Facebook documents a 200x200 minimum and Twitter's summary_large_image card documents 300x157, and nothing about reading the URL string tells you the image's actual pixel dimensions; that needs opening the file itself and reading its header, which is what this tool's CLI and standalone image checker do. (2) A relative og:image URL ("/images/share.png" instead of "https://example.com/images/share.png") renders fine if you click it in your own browser, because your browser resolves it against the page you're already on -- but the Open Graph protocol requires an absolute URL, and a platform's crawler fetching the tag value directly, with no page context to resolve it against, can fail silently. (3) A CMS plugin that writes its own og:title alongside a theme or hand-written one produces two tags with the same property name in the markup; which one a given platform's parser keeps is not something reading the HTML tells you, since both are sitting right there looking equally valid.

Why does the fallback chain matter here?

Platforms document a fallback: Twitter Cards fall back to the equivalent og:* tag when twitter:image, twitter:title, or twitter:description is absent, so a page missing twitter:image is not automatically broken on Twitter/X if og:image is set. Reading the markup by eye, a missing twitter:image tag looks like a problem -- and it's easy to "fix" by adding a duplicate image tag that then has to be kept in sync by hand. This tool applies the documented fallback chain before reporting anything as missing, so it only flags the case where the fallback itself has nothing to fall back to.

Open the Social Preview Checker to check your own page, or read the fallback chain and size-rule reference.

It is not a guarantee of how any individual platform will render the result today -- platforms cache aggressively and can change rendering rules without notice. A clean report describes what this one fetch found, not a promise about every platform's preview.

vs-facebook-sharing-debugger.html.text:
← Social Preview Checker

Social Preview Checker vs. Facebook Sharing Debugger

Different shapes: Facebook Sharing Debugger checks and refreshes Facebook's own cached view of one page, from Facebook's servers, and needs a Facebook login. This checker reads Open Graph and Twitter Card tags together, reads the preview image's real pixel dimensions, and needs no account -- as a browser report viewer or a matching CLI.

Check your page's tags →

Facebook Sharing Debugger, at developers.facebook.com/tools/debug, is Meta's own tool for checking how a URL will look when someone shares it on Facebook. You sign in with a Facebook account, paste a URL, and its own crawler fetches the page from Facebook's servers -- not from your browser -- then shows you the Open Graph tags that crawler read, a preview of the resulting share card, and a "Scrape Again" action that forces Facebook to re-fetch the page and refresh what it has cached for that URL. It is the tool Meta itself documents for diagnosing why a link looks wrong specifically on Facebook.

This checker does a broader, differently-shaped job. A CLI you run yourself (node cli/check.mjs <url> --json) sends one request to the page and its preview image, and the report covers both Open Graph and Twitter Card tags in one pass, applying the twitter:image/twitter:title/ twitter:description → og:* fallback chain platforms document rather than flagging a missing twitter:image as a problem on its own. It reads the preview image's real pixel dimensions straight out of the image file's own header -- not a cached crawler's account of them -- and a standalone tool on this page checks any image URL's real size with no CLI at all. No sign-in, no Facebook account, nothing uploaded to this site.

What each tool answers.
What you are trying to doWhere to do it
See exactly what Facebook's own crawler currently has cached for a URL, and force it to re-scrape after a fix. Facebook Sharing Debugger — it talks to Facebook's own cache directly, which this checker cannot do.
Get one report covering both Open Graph and Twitter Card tags, including the fallback chain between them, without a Facebook login. This checker — no account, and it checks both tag families in the same pass.
Know whether the preview image's actual pixel dimensions clear each platform's documented minimum, read from the image file itself rather than a crawler's report. This checker — the CLI reads the real header bytes, and the standalone browser tool checks any image URL directly.
Run the same check unattended in your own CI before a page ships. This checker's CLI, exit-code gateable — Facebook Sharing Debugger is an interactive, logged-in web tool.
Confirm how a link will actually render inside Facebook's own product surfaces today. Facebook Sharing Debugger — this checker only reads tags and image bytes; it does not talk to Facebook, X, or any platform's cache.

These compose rather than compete. A reasonable habit is this checker first, for a fast, account-free read across both tag families and the real image size before a page ships, and Facebook Sharing Debugger afterward when you specifically need to see or refresh what Facebook itself has cached for that exact URL.

Common questions

Should I use this checker or Facebook Sharing Debugger?

They overlap on one thing -- reading a page's Open Graph tags -- and differ in scope and how they get there. Facebook Sharing Debugger, at developers.facebook.com/tools/debug/, is Meta's own tool for checking how a URL will look when shared on Facebook: you sign in with a Facebook account, its own crawler fetches the page from Facebook's servers, and it shows the Open Graph tags that crawler read along with a preview card and a button to force Facebook to re-scrape the page and refresh its cache. This checker does a broader, differently-shaped job: a CLI you run yourself sends one request to the page and its preview image, reads Open Graph and Twitter Card tags together, applies the twitter:image to og:image fallback chain, and reads the image file's real pixel dimensions directly from its header rather than trusting a cached crawler's read -- with no Facebook account and no sign-in. Use Facebook Sharing Debugger when you specifically need to see or refresh Facebook's own cached preview of a page; use this checker when you want one report covering Open Graph and Twitter Card together, or a check you can wire into your own CI with no account involved.

Facebook Sharing Debugger is free too -- what does this add?

Being free is not the difference. Facebook Sharing Debugger requires signing in with a Facebook account before it will run at all, and what it shows you is scoped to Facebook's own crawler and Facebook's own cache of the page -- it does not check Twitter/X's card tags or fallback rules, and it reports the image dimensions its own crawler resolved rather than independently reading the image file's real pixel header. This checker needs no account of any kind, checks Open Graph and Twitter Card tags in the same report, applies the twitter:image/title/description to og:image/title/description fallback chain platforms document, and includes a standalone tool that reads any image URL's actual pixel dimensions straight from the file, with no crawler or cache in between. It also ships as a CLI, so the same check can run unattended in your own build pipeline.

Why does this need a CLI instead of one paste-a-URL box like Facebook Sharing Debugger?

Facebook Sharing Debugger can fetch an arbitrary URL because the fetch happens on Facebook's own servers, where cross-origin restrictions do not apply. A browser tab has no such privilege: fetching a third-party page's HTML from inside a page you're visiting is blocked by CORS unless that site opts in, which almost none do. A small local CLI, run from your own machine, does not have that restriction. The one piece that genuinely can run in any browser with no CLI is checking an image URL's real pixel dimensions, since loading an image via an img tag -- unlike fetching its bytes -- is not subject to CORS, which is what this page's standalone image-size tool uses.

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Meta Platforms, Inc. or Facebook. Facebook Sharing Debugger is a trademark of its owner, named here only to describe what this checker is and is not. What Facebook Sharing Debugger currently checks, and whether it requires a login, are described on Meta's own developer site -- check there for what it covers today.

vs-screamingfrog.html.text:
← Social Preview Checker

Social Preview Checker vs. Screaming Frog SEO Spider

Different jobs: one checks one page's link-preview tags in your browser right now, for free; the other crawls a whole site as an installed, paid desktop application.

Check a page →

Screaming Frog SEO Spider is a well-known SEO crawler, described on its own site (screamingfrog.co.uk) as a desktop application for Windows, macOS, and Linux that crawls an entire site and audits it against hundreds of checks -- broken links and response codes, page titles and meta descriptions, duplicate content, hreflang, XML sitemap generation, and extraction of social meta tags including Open Graph and Twitter Cards, among others, per its own documented feature list. Its free tier is capped at 500 URLs per crawl and leaves out advanced features such as JavaScript rendering, custom extraction, and saved crawl configurations; a paid annual license removes the crawl cap and unlocks those features.

That is a different job from the one this page does. This tool has no install, no crawl, and no per-site license. It exists for the narrower question that comes up when one specific page -- often one about to be shared or just published -- needs its link preview checked right now: will this page's Open Graph and Twitter Card tags actually produce a working preview, with a preview image that meets the platform's own documented size minimum?

What each tool answers.
QuestionWhere to answer it
Does this one page's og:image use a relative URL, and is the image actually large enough for Facebook's or Twitter's documented minimum? This checker — it reads the image file's own pixel dimensions and applies the platform-documented fallback chain, free, with nothing installed.
Crawl an entire site for broken links, duplicate titles, hreflang errors, and hundreds of other on-page SEO issues, with social tags as one part of that audit? Screaming Frog SEO Spider or a comparable crawler — a whole-site audit is a job this page does not attempt.
Check one page's link preview right before sharing it, with no install and no per-site crawl limit? This checker — paste the JSON from a small local CLI probe, or check just an image URL's real dimensions directly.
Keep a saved, repeatable crawl configuration across hundreds of pages and export the results? Screaming Frog SEO Spider or a comparable crawler — this page remembers nothing between visits except an anonymous local count of which features were used, and makes no claim to be a crawl archive.

This checker is deliberately the opposite shape from a site-wide crawler: nothing to install, nothing licensed per year, and nothing you paste here ever leaves your browser. That makes it a fast, honest answer for the one page in front of you — not a competitor to the whole-site audit a tool like Screaming Frog is built for.

Common questions

Should I use this checker or Screaming Frog SEO Spider?

They overlap on one narrow slice and differ everywhere else. Screaming Frog SEO Spider is a paid, installable desktop crawler (Windows, macOS, and Linux) that walks an entire site and reports on hundreds of things — broken links, response codes, titles and meta descriptions, duplicate content, hreflang, XML sitemaps, and, among its social-tag checks, Open Graph and Twitter Card extraction, per its own site. Its free tier is capped at 500 URLs per crawl and drops the advanced features (JavaScript rendering, custom extraction, saved crawl configs); a paid annual license removes that cap. This tool does one page at a time: paste the JSON from a small local CLI probe (or check a single image URL directly) and get a plain-English report on missing tags, a relative og:image URL, an image below a platform's documented minimum size, and the twitter:image to og:image fallback chain — free, in your browser, with nothing to install and no crawl limit because there is no crawl.

Does Screaming Frog already catch the problems this tool catches?

It extracts the same Open Graph and Twitter Card tags, per its own documented feature list, so a site-wide crawl will surface which pages have which tags set. What this tool adds is the specific classification: whether an og:image URL is relative (which the Open Graph protocol requires to be absolute), whether the image is actually large enough for Facebook's or Twitter's documented minimum — which needs reading the image file's own pixel dimensions, not just confirming a tag exists — and whether the twitter:image to og:image fallback chain leaves a page covered even without every tag set explicitly.

Why use a narrower tool if Screaming Frog already crawls the whole site?

Two reasons this tool exists alongside it. First, Screaming Frog is a desktop application you install and configure to crawl a site; this tool is a page you open and paste a small probe's JSON into, which is faster when you only care about the one URL in front of you right now — a page about to be shared, say — rather than auditing the whole domain. Second, this tool reads the preview image's real pixel dimensions from the image file's own header and checks them against the platform-specific minimums Facebook and Twitter document, which is a narrower, more specific answer than confirming a tag is present.

Is this page affiliated with Screaming Frog?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Screaming Frog Ltd. Screaming Frog is an independent company, named here only to describe what this checker is and is not, using facts drawn from its own public site at screamingfrog.co.uk.
